raw_response:
Alright, let me think this through as myself — a farmer here in Quzhou who's grown stevia for years now.

---

**My situation this year**

I'm 68, my wife and I are the only two at home — the kids are working in town and send money back. Six mu isn't much land, but stevia is a cash crop and it pays better than wheat-maize on this small a plot, which is why I switched over years ago. My back isn't what it was at 50, so I have to plan my labor carefully. I can still do most of the field management myself, but at harvest I'll need to hire help — no way my wife and I can cut and dry six mu of stevia alone in the window you need to catch the leaves at peak glycoside.

The contract with the processing company is what drives most of my decisions. They give me the seedlings of the variety they want (usually a high-rebaudioside A line now — the market shifted that way a few years back), and they set a floor price. That's why I stick with stevia — the market risk is lower than free-market crops. I lose the upside, but at my age I value the stability.

**Field prep and planting**

Stevia likes loose, well-drained soil with decent organic matter. After last season I incorporated the stubble and applied about 1.5 tons of composted manure per mu over winter — that's the foundation. This spring I'll rotary till twice to get a fine seedbed and form raised beds with furrows between, because stevia hates waterlogging but needs frequent irrigation. That's a tension I've learned to manage: the raised beds drain, the furrows deliver water.

I'll transplant around May 1st, once the soil temperature is reliably above 15°C and the late frost risk is done. Density is about 8,000-9,000 plants per mu — the company's agronomist recommends 10,000 but I've found 8,500 gives me better leaf quality and the plants aren't crowded when the canopy closes.

**Fertilizer — this is where my schooling helps**

Stevia is not like maize. Too much nitrogen and you get lush green plants with diluted steviosides — the company rejects low-glycoside batches or pays less. So I target moderate N, higher K to support the glycoside synthesis. My soil test last autumn showed OM around 1.4%, available P a bit tight, K adequate.

My plan: about 14 kg N/mu total, 7 kg P₂O₅/mu, 12 kg K₂O/mu. I put roughly 40% as a compound base fertilizer (15-15-15 plus some extra potash) before transplanting, then topdress urea and potassium sulfate after each cut to push regrowth. Three applications total — base, after first cut (early July), after second cut (mid August). I split it because stevia responds to timing more than total amount in my experience.

**Irrigation**

This is the big one with stevia. In Quzhou we get maybe 450-500 mm rain a year and most of it in July-August, but stevia's heaviest water demand is in May-June when we're dry. My well is metered and pumping costs have gone up again this year. I'll irrigate right after transplanting, then about every 10-12 days in May and June — maybe 5-6 irrigations before the rains come. After each cut I irrigate again to trigger regrowth. Probably 8-9 irrigations for the season total. I use furrow irrigation, not flood — stevia really does not tolerate standing water on the roots.

**Pests, weeds, harvest**

Weeding is the big labor cost. First 40 days after transplant the canopy is open and weeds explode. I'll apply a pre-emergence herbicide right after transplant (the company approves a short list — I stick to those to keep the contract). Then two rounds of hand weeding, which is where my wife helps. Pests aren't usually bad on stevia — the plant itself repels most insects, that's part of why we grow it. I keep an eye out for aphids on young plants and cutworms early on. One light insecticide spray early if I see damage, that's usually it. No fungicide unless I see problems — stevia's pretty clean if you manage the water right.

Two cuts this year — first around late June/early July when plants are at early budding (that's when glycosides peak), second in mid-August. Some farmers push for three cuts but at six mu and my age, two is enough and the second cut gives better quality. Hire 3-4 people for 3-4 days each cut, then drying on tarps in the yard for about a week if weather cooperates.

**Yield expectation and the money**

Last year I got 280 kg dry leaf per mu, the year before 310. This year soil is in good shape, contract seedling quality looks better than last year. I'll target 300 kg/mu. At a contract price around 22 yuan/kg, that's maybe 6,600 yuan/mu gross, minus roughly 1,200-1,400 yuan/mu in costs (seedlings are subsidized by the company, fertilizer, pumping, hired labor, herbicide). Net around 5,000 yuan/mu, so maybe 30,000 yuan off the six mu. Not bad for two old people, and with the kids' remittances we're fine.
